**The Commentary on Surah al-Kawthar**, which is Meccan according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and Medinan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah. It has three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar.﴾ (1)

On this verse there are two issues.

**The first:** the Exalted's statement, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾. This is the recitation of the majority: *inna a'taynaka* with the letter *ʿayn*. Al-Hasan and Talhah ibn Musarrif read *anṭaynāka* with the letter *nūn*, and Umm Salamah related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is a dialectal form for giving: *anṭaytuhu* means *a'ṭaytuhu*, "I gave him." *Al-Kawthar* is of the pattern *fawʿal* from *al-kathrah* (abundance), like *al-nawfal* from *al-nafl* and *al-jawhar* from *al-jahr*. The Arabs call anything abundant in number, quantity or value a *kawthar*. Sufyan said: it was said to an old woman whose son had returned from a journey, "With what has your son returned?" She said, "With a *kawthar*," meaning with abundant wealth. A *kawthar* among men is a lord who is abundant in goodness. al-Kumayt said:

*"You are abundant, O son of Marwan, and good,*
*And your father was the son of noble women, a kawthar."*

*Al-kawthar* also means a large number of companions and supporters, and *al-kawthar* of dust means a great quantity of it. *Takawthara* means it became abundant. A poet said:

*"The dust of death has risen until it became abundant."*

[[This is the second half of a line by Hassan ibn Nashbah. Its first half, as in al-Lisan, is:
"They refused to give up their neighbour to their enemy."]]

**The second:** the people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed about the *kawthar* that was given to the Prophet (ﷺ), into sixteen opinions.

The first: it is a river in Paradise. al-Bukhari related it from Anas, and al-Tirmidhi too, and we have mentioned it in the book *al-Tadhkirah*. al-Tirmidhi also related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*al-Kawthar* is a river in Paradise, whose banks are of gold, whose course is over pearls and rubies, whose soil is more fragrant than musk, whose water is sweeter than honey and whiter than snow." This is a *hadith* that is *hasan sahih* (good and sound).

The second: it is the Prophet's (ﷺ) Basin (*hawd*) at the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by 'Ata'. In Sahih Muslim, from Anas, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one day among us, he dozed off briefly, then raised his head smiling. We said, 'What made you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'A surah was just revealed to me,' and he recited: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾' Then he said: 'Do you know what al-Kawthar is?' We said, 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a river which my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has promised me. On it is much good. It is a basin to which my Ummah will come on the Day of Resurrection, whose vessels are as numerous as the stars. A servant (of Allah) will be pulled away from them, and I will say: "He is from my Ummah," and it will be said: "You do not know what he innovated after you."'"

[[In the Sahih, the text reads: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was once among us one day, and he dozed off..." and so on until the end of the hadith.]]

The reports about his Basin at the place of standing are numerous, and we have mentioned them in the book *al-Tadhkirah*. Upon its four corners are the four Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all. Whoever hates one of them will not be given to drink by the other. We have mentioned there who will be driven away from it, so whoever wishes to know about that should reflect upon it there.

Then it is permissible to call that river or basin *kawthar*, because of the great number of those who come to it and drink from it from the Ummah of Muhammad (peace be upon him) there, and it is named so for the abundant good and abundant water in it.

The third: *al-Kawthar* is prophethood and the Book. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

The fourth: it is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: it is Islam. This was related by al-Mughirah.

The sixth: the facilitation of the Qur'an and the lightening of the laws (*shara'i'*). This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The seventh: it is the abundance of companions, of the Ummah, and of followers. This was said by Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash and Yaman ibn Ri'ab.

The eighth: it is preferring others (*al-iythar*). This was said by Ibn Kaysan.

The ninth: it is the elevation of remembrance. This was related by al-Mawardi.

The tenth: it is a light in your heart that guides you to Me and cuts you off from other than Me. It is also reported from him that it is intercession (*al-shafa'ah*), and that is the eleventh. It was also said: the miracles of the Lord by which those who respond to your call are guided. This was related by al-Tha'labi, and that is the twelfth.

The thirteenth: Hilal ibn Yasaf said: it is "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." It was also said: it is understanding of the religion (*al-fiqh fi al-din*). It was also said: it is the five daily prayers. These two are the fourteenth and fifteenth. Ibn Ishaq said: it is the great matter. He cited the verse of Labid:

*"And a companion of Mulhub, we mourned his loss,*
*And at the parting there was another kawthar."*

That is, a great one.

[[Mulhub: a water belonging to the Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah. Its companion: 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas. Al-Radda' (with a kasrah) is also the name of a water. Al-kawthar also means an abundantly good lord.]]

I say: the most correct of these opinions are the first and the second, because it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly concerning the *kawthar*. Anas heard a group discussing the Basin, and he said: "I did not think I would live to see people like you disputing about the Basin. I have left behind me old women, none of whom prays without asking Allah to give her to drink from the Basin of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Regarding his Basin, a poet says:

*"O master of the Basin, who can come near you?*
*And you are truly the beloved of the Creator."*

All that has been said after this regarding its interpretation is in addition to the fact that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given his Basin, may abundant peace be upon him.

In it there are five issues. The first concerns His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So pray﴾, meaning: establish the obligatory prayer upon you. Al-Dahhak narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah said: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ refers to the 'Id prayer and the day of sacrifice, and ﴿and sacrifice﴾ means sacrifice your offerings (nusuk). Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sacrifice and then pray, so he was commanded to pray and then sacrifice. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: ﴿Pray to your Lord﴾ refers to the obligatory dawn prayer at Jam' [[Jam': al-Muzdalifah.]], and ﴿sacrifice the camels﴾ refers to sacrificing at Mina. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: It was revealed at Hudaybiyyah when the Prophet (ﷺ) was prevented from reaching the House. So Allah commanded him to pray, sacrifice the camels, and return, and he did so.

Ibn al-Arabi said: As for those who said that what is meant by His saying ﴿So pray﴾ is the five daily prayers, they are the pillar of worship, the foundation of Islam, and the greatest of the supports of the religion. As for those who said it is the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah, that is because it is joined with the sacrifice, which takes place on that day, and no other prayer is performed on that day before the sacrifice. So it was singled out from among the prayers for mention because it is joined with the sacrifice.

I say: As for those who said it is the 'Id prayer, that is outside Makkah, since there is no 'Id prayer in Makkah by consensus (ijma'), as related by Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "As for Malik, he said: I have not heard anything about it. What occurs to my mind is that what is meant is the prayer of the day of sacrifice, and the sacrifice follows it." 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The meaning is to place the right hand upon the left opposite the chest (nahr) during prayer. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also narrated from 'Ali: that one should raise his hands in the takbir up to his chest. Likewise Ja'far ibn 'Ali said regarding ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾: he raises his hands when he first says the takbir of entry into the prayer, up to the chest.

It is related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: When ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this sacrifice (nahirah) that Allah has commanded me with?" He said: "It is not a sacrifice, but He commands you that when you begin the prayer with the takbir, you raise your hands when you say the takbir, when you raise your head from ruku', and when you prostrate. Indeed, it is our prayer and the prayer of the angels who are in the seven heavens. Every thing has an adornment, and the adornment of the prayer is the raising of the hands at every takbir."

It is related from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: Face the qiblah with your chest (nahr). This was also said by al-Farra', al-Kalbi and Abu al-Ahwas.

From this is the verse of the poet:

"O Abu Hakam, you are not the paternal uncle of Mujalid
and the lord of the people of al-Abtah, the one who faces (you)."

That is, the one who is opposite. Al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs say: "Our dwellings face one another (tatanahar)," meaning: this one's chest is opposite that one's chest, i.e., it is across from it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is a man standing in prayer facing the mihrab, from their saying "their dwellings face one another," i.e., they are opposite one another.

It is related from 'Ata' that he said: He was commanded to sit upright between the two prostrations until his chest (nahr) appears. Sulayman al-Taymi said: That is, raise your hand in supplication up to your chest. It was also said: the meaning of "So pray" is: worship. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: ﴿Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, meaning: indeed some people pray to other than Allah and sacrifice to other than Allah, but We have given you al-Kawthar, so let neither your prayer nor your sacrifice be except for Allah.

Ibn al-Arabi said: What I think is that He intended: worship your Lord and sacrifice to Him, so let your deed be only for the One who has singled you out with al-Kawthar. It is most fitting (hari) that all the deed should match this special favour of al-Kawthar, which is abundant good that Allah has given you, or the river whose clay is musk and whose drinking vessels are as many as the stars of heaven. As for matching this with the prayer of the day of sacrifice and the slaughter of a ram, a cow or a camel, that is far-fetched in measure and in arrangement, and in balancing the reward against the act of worship.

And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The discussion about the sacrifice and its virtue and the time of its slaughter has already passed in the commentary on Surah "as-Saffat" [[See vol. 15, p. 107 and what follows.]], so there is no point in repeating it. We also mentioned a number of its rulings in Surah "al-Hajj" [[See vol. 12, p. 42 and what follows.]].

Ibn al-Arabi said: Among the strange matters is that al-Shafi'i said: Whoever sacrifices before the prayer, it suffices him. Yet Allah, the Exalted, says in His Book: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, so He began with the prayer before the sacrifice. The Prophet (ﷺ) said (in al-Bukhari and others, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said): "The first thing we begin with on this day of ours is to pray, then return and sacrifice. Whoever does this has done our rite correctly, and whoever slaughters before that has merely offered meat to his family, which is not part of the rite at all." His companions deny this, and how good is agreement!

The third issue: As for what was related from 'Ali (peace be upon him) concerning ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, that it means placing the right hand upon the left in prayer, this was transmitted by al-Daraqutni. Our scholars differed on this in three opinions.

The first: it is not placed, neither in an obligatory prayer nor in a supererogatory (nafilah) one, because that is a form of leaning (i'timad), which is not permitted in the obligatory prayer and not recommended in the supererogatory one.

The second: it is not done in the obligatory prayer, but it is done in the supererogatory prayer for assistance, because that is a place of leniency.

The third: it is done in both the obligatory and the supererogatory prayer. This is the correct view, because it is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his right hand upon his left, from the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr and others.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: This was the view of Malik, Ahmad and Ishaq, and it is reported from al-Shafi'i. The people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) regarded it as recommended. A group held that the hands should be let hang (irsal al-yad). Among those from whom we have this reported is Ibn al-Mundhir: and al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. I say: It is also related from Malik. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Letting the hands hang and placing the right over the left are both part of the sunnah (prophetic practice) of prayer.

The fourth: they differed about the place where the hand is placed. It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he placed them upon his chest. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: above the navel. And one said: there is no harm if it is below the navel. A group said: it is placed below the navel. This was related from 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, al-Nakha'i and Abu Mijlaz, and Sufyan al-Thawri and Ishaq held this view.

The fifth: As for raising the hands while saying the takbir at the opening, at ruku', at rising from ruku', and at prostration, there is disagreement about this. Al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Humayd, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raise his hands when he entered the prayer, when he bowed, when he raised his head from bowing, and when he prostrated. Only 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi transmitted it from Humayd as a marfu' (prophetic) report, and the correct view is that it is from the action of Anas.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he stood to pray, raise his hands until they were level with his shoulders, then say the takbir. He would do the same when he said the takbir for ruku', and would do the same when he raised his head from ruku', saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." He would not do it when he raised his head from prostration. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. Ibn Wahb related this view from Malik. There are other views, but this is the one established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Another group said: the worshipper raises his hands only when he begins the prayer, and does not raise them at any other time. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri and the people of opinion.

I say: This is also the well-known position of the school of Malik, based on the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, which al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il, who said: Muhammad ibn Jabir narrated to us from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from 'Alqamah, from 'Abd Allah, who said: I prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ), with Abu Bakr and with 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), and they did not raise their hands except at the first takbir at the beginning of the prayer. Ishaq said: We adopt this for the whole prayer. Al-Daraqutni said: Muhammad ibn Jabir (who was weak) alone transmitted it from Hammad, from Ibrahim. Others than Hammad transmit it from Ibrahim as mursal, from 'Abd Allah, as his own action, not raised (marfu') to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the correct version.

Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from al-Bara', that he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) when he began the prayer raise his hands until they reached his ears, and then he did not return to that until he finished the prayer. Al-Daraqutni said: Yazid was taught the phrase "then he did not return" in the last part of his life, so he accepted it, and he had become confused (ikhtalata).

In Mukhtasar ma laysa fi al-Mukhtasar (the abridgment of what is not in the Mukhtasar), it is related from Malik: he does not raise his hands during any part of the prayer. Ibn al-Qasim said: I did not see Malik raise his hands at the opening takbir (al-ihram). He said: And the most beloved to me is abandoning the raising of the hands at the opening takbir.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 108, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾ That is, the one who hates you, and he is Al-‘As ibn Wa'il. The Arabs used to call a man who had sons and daughters, but then his sons died and only his daughters remained, "abtar" (cut off, without posterity). It is said that Al-‘As stood with the Prophet ﷺ speaking with him, and a group of the chieftains of Quraysh said to him: "With whom were you standing?" He said: "With that abtar." Before that, ʿAbd Allah, the son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Khadijah, had died. So Allah, exalted is His majesty, revealed: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, meaning the one whose remembrance is cut off from the good of this world and the Hereafter.

ʿIkrimah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah, when a man's son died, would say: 'So-and-so has been cut off.' When Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet ﷺ, died, Abu Jahl went out to his companions and said: 'Muhammad has been cut off.' So Allah, may His praise be exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, meaning by that Abu Jahl."

Shimr ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt.

It is also said that Quraysh used to say of a man whose male offspring had died: "So-and-so has been cut off." When the son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, al-Qasim, died in Makkah, and Ibrahim in Madinah, they said: "Muhammad has been cut off; there is no one to take up his affair after him." So this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

It is also said that it was a reply to Quraysh when they said to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, when he came to Makkah: "We are the people of the water-providing, the custodianship of the Kaʿbah, the chamberlainship, and the banner, and you are the chief of the people of Madinah. Are we better, or this Sunaybir (in another copy: Sunbur; its meaning will be explained by the author), the cut-off one of his people?" Kaʿb said: "Rather, you are better." So concerning Kaʿb was revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in idols and false deities?﴾ [al-Nisa': 51] and the verse. And concerning Quraysh was revealed: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, as Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah also said.

It is also said that when Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed to His Messenger and he called Quraysh to faith, they said: "Muhammad has been cut off from us," meaning he opposed us and separated from us. So Allah, exalted, informed His Messenger ﷺ that they are the ones who are cut off. This was also said by ʿIkrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab.

The lexicographers said: "Al-abtar among men is the one who has no son, and among animals the one who has no tail. Every matter from which the good trace has been cut off is abtar. Al-batr means cutting: batartu al-shay' batran, I cut it before completion. Al-inbitar means severance. Al-batir is the cutting sword. Al-abtar is the one whose tail is cut off; one says of it: butira [with kasra] yubtaru batran. In a hadith: 'What is this al-buteira?' Ziyad delivered his sermon, the 'batra' sermon, because he did not praise Allah in it and did not invoke blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "Al-abtaran are the mule and the slave; they were called abtarayn because of the scarcity of their good." And Allah has made him abtar: that is, made him cut off. It is said: rajul ubatir (with a damma on the hamza): the one who severs his kinship ties. The poet said:

"A base man, in whose nose a sore has broken out, / upon severing a near kinsman, a cutter of ties."

Al-Butariyyah is a sect of the Zaydiyyah, attributed to al-Mughirah ibn Saʿd, whose epithet was al-Abtar. As for al-Sunbur, it is a shared (homonymous) term. It is said: it is the palm tree left standing alone, whose base is pounded and stripped; one says: sanbara asfal al-nakhlah (the base of the palm tree became sunbur). It is also said: it is the solitary man who has no son and no brother. It is also said: it is specifically the outlet of a basin, reported by Abu ʿUbayd, and he recited:

"Between a sunbur and the al-izaʾ"

And al-sunbur is a reed that is in a water-vessel of iron or lead from which one drinks. Al-Jawhari, may Allah have mercy on him, related all of this. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.
